The objective of this internship energy audit is to systematically
monitor and analyse the energy performance of Air Compressor No. 2
GA30VSD (Atlas Copco). over a 21-day period. The study focuses on:

-   Monitoring daily load factor, current draw, delivery pressure, and
    discharge temperature over 21 consecutive days.

-   Calculating the compressor\'s Specific Power (kW/m³/min) using
    nameplate data and benchmarking against BEE standards.

-   Quantifying the energy and cost saving potential if performance is
    below the BEE benchmark.

-   Reviewing the plant\'s electricity bills for power factor and
    maximum demand performance.

-   Recommending practical, low-investment corrective actions to improve
    compressor efficiency and reduce energy costs.

This audit covers the following areas:

-   Air Compressor No. 2 GA30VSD (Atlas Copco) --- load factor
    monitoring, specific power calculation, and benchmarking against BEE
    standards.

-   Electricity bill review --- power factor, maximum demand, and unit
    cost analysis.

The audit does not cover other compressors, process-side pneumatic
systems, or compressed air distribution network leak quantification,
which are recommended as scope for a follow-on detailed audit.

The audit followed a structured data-collection and analysis approach
based on BEE (Bureau of Energy Efficiency) guidelines:

-   Daily compressor log sheet readings were recorded for 21 consecutive
    days from in-plant operator log books.

-   Parameters recorded each day: average load %, average current
    (amps), delivery pressure (kg/cm²), and average discharge
    temperature (°C).

-   Daily averages were computed from hourly readings taken by the plant
    operator each shift.

-   Nameplate data obtained: Motor Rated Power = 30 kW (40 HP); FAD at 7
    bar = 3.10 m³/min (Atlas Copco GA30VSD specification).

-   Specific Power computed as: Actual Power (kW) = Rated kW × (Avg
    Load% ÷ 100); Specific Power = Actual Power ÷ FAD (m³/min).

-   Result benchmarked against BEE standard: 4.5--5.0 kW/m³/min = good
    performance; above 5.5 kW/m³/min = significant efficiency gap.

-   Annual saving estimated at 8,000 operating hours/year (24 hr/day ×
    330 days/year) and unit rate from electricity bill.

Specific Power (kW/m³/min) is the standard BEE metric for compressor
efficiency --- lower is better. It measures how much power is consumed
per unit volume of free air delivered.

**Specific Power = (Rated Motor kW × Avg Load% ÷ 100) ÷ FAD (m³/min)**

An indicative specific power of 7.26 kW/m³/min was estimated using
average load factor and nameplate FAD. Actual compressor efficiency
should be verified using measured power consumption and airflow,
compared with the BEE benchmark range of 4.5--5.0 kW/m³/min. This
indicates that the compressor may be consuming more power than expected
for the volume of compressed air delivered.

The difference between the calculated value and the benchmark
corresponds to an estimated excess power requirement of approximately
7.0 kW under the observed operating conditions. Based on the compressor
operating schedule of 7,920 hours per year, this excess power
corresponds to an annual energy consumption of approximately 55,440
kWh/year.

Therefore, the identified saving should be considered a realistic
improvement opportunity rather than an immediate guaranteed reduction in
electricity cost.

-   Air Compressor No. 1 GA30VSD (Atlas Copco) operated at an average
    load factor of 75% over 21 days. The Variable Speed Drive (VSD)
    design allows the motor to match speed to demand, which is more
    efficient than fixed-speed machines at part load.

-   Calculated specific power of 7.26 kW/m³/min is significantly above
    the BEE benchmark of 4.5--5.0 kW/m³/min --- indicating that the
    compressor is consuming more power per unit of air delivered than
    the benchmark standard. This gap warrants investigation into root
    causes.

-   Delivery pressure remained constant at 6.7 kg/cm² across all 21 days
    --- indicating stable process demand. However, any excess pressure
    above actual process needs directly raises specific power and should
    be reviewed.

-   Average discharge temperature of 96°C is within normal range. Three
    days (Days 6, 17, and 19) recorded 100--102°C --- elevated
    temperatures can indicate oil cooler fouling or high ambient
    conditions and should be monitored.

-   Two power cut events (Days 5 and 20) and one power loss shutdown
    (Day 11) were recorded --- these are external events and do not
    affect the efficiency assessment.

-   Day 6 (blow moulding activity) showed higher current draw (110 A)
    consistent with elevated compressed air demand from that process.

-   Investigate why specific power (7.26 kW/m³/min) is above BEE
    benchmark. The VSD design of the GA30VSD should theoretically
    perform closer to 5.0 kW/m³/min --- the gap suggests one or more of
    the following root causes.

-   Check inlet air filter condition --- a choked inlet filter increases
    specific power by forcing the compressor to work harder for the same
    air output. Replace filter element if pressure drop across it
    exceeds the manufacturer\'s limit (typically 35--50 mbar).

-   Check compressed air distribution network for leaks --- each
    undetected leak forces the compressor to run longer and harder. A
    simple ultrasonic leak detection survey is recommended; leaks
    typically account for 10--30% of compressor output in plants of this
    type.

-   Review delivery pressure setting --- confirm that 6.7 kg/cm² is the
    minimum required by all end-use equipment. Every 1 kg/cm² reduction
    saves approximately 6--8% compressor energy. Reducing to 6.0 kg/cm²
    (if process allows) would save approximately 5--6 kWh per operating
    hour.

-   Verify VSD controller pressure band settings --- ensure the setpoint
    and deadband in the Atlas Copco controller are correctly configured
    for minimum energy operation at actual process demand.

-   Clean oil cooler fins if fouled --- three days recorded discharge
    temperatures of 100--102°C (Days 6, 17, 19). Fouled oil cooler
    raises discharge temperature, degrades oil life, and risks thermal
    shutdown.

-   Check ventilation in the compressor room --- high ambient
    temperature is a common cause of elevated discharge temperature in
    enclosed plant rooms.

-   If power factor is below 0.95: install or upgrade APFC (Automatic
    Power Factor Correction) panel --- low investment, typically 1--2
    year payback.

-   If maximum demand exceeds sanctioned limit: stagger equipment
    startups to avoid MD penalties.

-   Electricity billing is on a kVAh basis at Rs. 6/kVAh. Power Factor
    recorded at 0.99 --- no APFC action required. Maximum Demand
    recorded at 2088 kVA against a sanctioned limit of 2800 kVA --- no
    MD penalty applies.

To validate the findings of this study and accurately quantify
recoverable savings, the following activities are recommended:

-   Install temporary power analyzer for minimum seven days.

-   Conduct ultrasonic compressed-air leak survey.

-   Verify end-use pressure requirements.

-   Measure actual compressor airflow.

-   Compare measured specific power against BEE benchmark.

-   Recalculate annual savings based on measured data.

The audit has successfully established an operating performance baseline
for Air Compressor No. 2 and identified measurable opportunities for
improving compressed-air system efficiency Preliminary analysis
indicates a potential energy-saving opportunity of approximately 55,440
kWh/year (₹4.43 lakh/year), which should be validated through airflow
and power measurement before implementation.The identified opportunity
is technically achievable through systematic investigation of leakage
losses, pressure optimization, maintenance practices, and compressor
control settings.

The compressor operated reliably over the 21-day audit period with a
consistent average load factor of 75% and stable delivery pressure of
6.7 kg/cm². The three events of elevated discharge temperature
(100--102°C on Days 6, 17, and 19) warrant monitoring and preventive
maintenance of the oil cooler system.

The primary corrective actions recommended are: inlet filter
maintenance, compressed air leak detection, delivery pressure
optimisation, and VSD controller setting verification. These are
low-cost, high-return interventions that do not require capital
investment in new equipment.

This audit establishes a systematic energy monitoring baseline for the
compressed air system. Extending the scope to include distribution
network leak quantification and demand-side audit is recommended as the
next phase.

Average current recorded during the audit was 102 A. Current readings
were used as supporting operational data; however, accurate power
consumption measurement would require a calibrated power analyzer.

boiler by analysing operating data recorded over a 21-day period (1 June
-- 21 June 2026). The focus areas are flue gas temperature trend, steam
generation consistency, and development of production-normalised energy
performance indicators (EnPIs) that can serve as a baseline for future
monitoring.

The boiler achieved 189.5°C on 17 June under normal operating
conditions, confirming that this lower flue gas temperature is
attainable. On 20 of the 21 days monitored, flue gas temperature
exceeded this value, indicating a sustained and recoverable condition
\--Potentially attributable to economiser fouling, air preheater
fouling, excess air operation, combustion variation, or other
heat-transfer-related factors requiring further investigation

The 0.75% efficiency loss is estimated using the BEE thumb rule (1%
efficiency loss per 22°C excess flue gas temperature). This is a widely
used indicative rule, not a result of direct efficiency testing. A
proper boiler efficiency test using the indirect method (as per BEE
guidelines) with measured fuel GCV, proximate analysis, and flue gas
composition would be required to confirm this figure.

Average steam generation was 13.65 TPH, resulting in an estimated daily
steam output of 327.6 tonnes (13.65 × 24 hrs). Steam generation remained
within the normal operating range of approximately 12--16 TPH, except
for the shutdown event recorded on 21 June.

1.  Average flue gas exit temperature over the 21-day monitoring period

2.  The boiler demonstrated a minimum flue gas temperature of 189.5°C on

    normal operating conditions.

3.  The 16.4°C gap between the average and the best-demonstrated
    temperature corresponds to an indicative efficiency loss of \~0.75%

    isolated event.

4.  No financial or fuel savings are claimed in this report. The
    efficiency opportunity is expressed in physical terms only, pending

5.  Baseline EnPIs have been established: 0.97 t steam per tonne of
    product; 195 kg rice husk per tonne of product. These provide a
    reference for future performance tracking.

Inspect and clean economiser tube surfaces at the next planned
maintenance shutdown. Soot and ash deposits reduce heat transfer and
directly raise flue gas exit temperature. Schedule on the basis of the
temperature trend observed in this report.

Inspect air preheater (APH) surfaces for fouling, tube leakage, ash
accumulation, and bypass damper condition. Confirm whether an APH is
fitted and operational.

Review combustion settings and flue gas O₂/CO₂ readings. High excess air
independently raises flue gas temperature and dry flue gas losses,
separate from surface fouling.

section: Recommendation 4: Install or Verify Fuel Metering
text:
To enable credible energy accounting and savings verification, install a
calibrated rice husk weighbridge or flow meter. The current audit relies
on a plant-stated 66 t/day figure. Without verified fuel consumption,
neither specific energy consumption nor financial savings can be
formally claimed.

Perform a full indirect boiler efficiency test per BEE guidelines ---
including flue gas analysis (CO₂, O₂, CO), fuel proximate analysis (GCV,
moisture, ash), and radiation/convection loss estimation. This will
replace the indicative 0.75% estimate with a verified efficiency figure.

Track the following indicators monthly:

-   Flue gas exit temperature should be monitored against the
    demonstrated benchmark of 189.5°C while maintaining required steam
    generation and process demand.

Over the 21-day monitoring period, the boiler\'s average flue gas exit
temperature of 205.9°C exceeded its own best-demonstrated performance of
189.5°C (recorded on 17 June) by 16.4°C. This gap indicates a sustained
and This gap indicates a sustained opportunity for improvement in boiler
thermal performance and warrants further investigation.

Using the BEE indicative rule, this corresponds to approximately 0.75%
thermal efficiency loss. No financial savings figure has been stated in
this report, as the fuel consumption data has not been independently
verified and no direct efficiency test was conducted during the audit
period.

The recommended actions --- economiser and APH cleaning, excess air
review, fuel metering installation, and periodic KPI tracking --- are
low-cost, high-return measures. Their impact should be quantified
through a verified before-and-after measurement exercise.

Why this audit
Establish a measured performance baseline for two major energy-consuming utilities: the compressed-air system and the biomass boiler.
Benchmark current performance against Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) standards and the equipment's own best-demonstrated performance.
Quantify indicative energy and cost saving potential where performance falls outside benchmark ranges.
Recommend practical, low-investment corrective actions that do not require new capital equipment.
Define a validation phase — metering and testing — needed before savings are formally claimed.
Common methodology basis
Daily log-sheet readings recorded by plant operators for 21 consecutive days (1–21 June 2026), from in-plant data — not independently metered during the audit.
Daily averages computed from hourly shift readings; nameplate/datasheet specifications used for rated capacity figures.
Performance benchmarked against BEE Energy Audit Guidelines and Guide Book 3 — Electrical Utilities.
Annual saving / efficiency-loss estimates are scaled using standard operating-hour assumptions and BEE thumb rules, and flagged for follow-up verification.
Each system audit follows the same structure: equipment profile → 21-day data → performance analysis → findings → recommendations.

VSD Advantage
A Variable Speed Drive compressor matches motor speed to real-time air demand, which is inherently more efficient than fixed-speed machines at part load — making it a useful candidate for specific-power benchmarking.
Why Specific Power Matters
Specific Power (kW per m³/min of delivered air) is the standard BEE metric for compressor efficiency — lower is better. It normalises power draw against actual air output, enabling fair benchmarking regardless of compressor size.

Key Observations
Average load factor of 75% over 21 days. The VSD design allows the motor to match speed to demand — inherently more efficient than fixed-speed machines at part load.
Calculated specific power of 7.26 kW/m³/min is significantly above the BEE benchmark of 4.5–5.0 — indicating the compressor consumes more power per unit of air delivered than the standard, warranting root-cause investigation.
Delivery pressure remained constant at 6.7 kg/cm² across all 21 days, indicating stable process demand. Any excess pressure above actual process needs directly raises specific power.
Average discharge temperature of 96°C is within normal range. Three days (6, 17, 19) recorded 100–102°C — possible oil-cooler fouling or high ambient conditions to monitor.
Two power-cut events (Days 5, 20) and one power-loss shutdown (Day 11) were recorded — external events that do not affect the efficiency assessment.
Day 6 (blow-moulding activity) showed higher current draw (110 A), consistent with elevated compressed-air demand from that process.

SECTION A · COMPRESSOR
Recommendations
Priority Actions — Specific Power
Check inlet air filter condition. Replace if pressure drop exceeds 35–50 mbar — a choked filter forces the compressor to work harder for the same air output.
Conduct an ultrasonic compressed-air leak survey. Undetected leaks typically account for 10–30% of compressor output in plants of this type.
Review the delivery pressure setpoint. Every 1 kg/cm² reduction saves ~6–8% compressor energy; reducing 6.7→6.0 kg/cm² (if process allows) saves ~5–6 kWh per operating hour.
Verify VSD controller pressure-band settings — confirm setpoint and deadband are configured for minimum-energy operation at actual process demand.
Maintenance & Electrical
Clean oil cooler fins if fouled — raised discharge temp degrades oil life and risks thermal shutdown.
Check compressor-room ventilation — high ambient temperature is a common cause of elevated discharge temperature.
Next-Phase Validation
Install a temporary power analyzer for minimum 7 days.
Conduct ultrasonic leak survey & verify end-use pressure needs.
Measure actual airflow; recompute specific power against BEE benchmark and recalculate annual savings.

SECTION B · BOILER
Recommendations
1. Economiser Cleaning
Inspect and clean economiser tube surfaces at the next planned maintenance shutdown — soot and ash deposits reduce heat transfer and directly raise flue gas exit temperature.
2. Air Preheater Inspection
Inspect APH surfaces for fouling, tube leakage, ash accumulation, and bypass damper condition; confirm whether an APH is fitted and operational.
3. Excess Air Optimisation
Review combustion settings and flue gas O₂/CO₂ readings — high excess air independently raises flue gas temperature and dry flue gas losses.
4. Install / Verify Fuel Metering
Install a calibrated rice-husk weighbridge or flow meter. Without verified fuel consumption, neither specific energy consumption nor financial savings can be formally claimed.
5. Conduct Indirect Efficiency Test
Full indirect boiler efficiency test per BEE guidelines — flue gas analysis, fuel proximate analysis, radiation/convection loss estimation — to replace the indicative 0.75% estimate.
6. Monthly KPI Tracking
Track flue gas temp vs. the 189.5°C benchmark, rice husk per tonne of steam/product, and steam per tonne of product on a monthly basis.

Limitations & Data Gaps
These limitations apply to this report and should be addressed before any savings figure is formally claimed or submitted for energy audit compliance purposes.

1 | Fuel consumption not independently measured | 66 t/day is plant-stated — no weighbridge or flow-meter verification. Cost and SEC figures are indicative only.
2 | Fuel GCV not lab-tested | Standard reference GCV of 3,200 kcal/kg assumed; actual GCV varies with moisture/quality. Lab-tested GCV needed.
3 | No boiler efficiency test conducted | 0.75% loss is from the BEE thumb rule, not a direct test. Indirect-method test required to confirm.
4 | Flue gas temp. is the only heat-loss parameter measured | Unburnt carbon, radiation/convection, blow-down, and fuel-moisture losses are not quantified.
5 | Manufacturer design flue gas temp. not confirmed | Benchmark used is the boiler's own best day (189.5°C) — conservative; design figure may show a larger gap.
6 | No pre/post measurement after cleaning | A before/after flue gas temperature comparison at the same load is needed to verify actual improvement.
7 | 21 June anomaly | Steam flow dropped to 8.3 TPH due to a logged shutdown — retained in dataset but not representative.

Conclusion
Air Compressor
Established an operating performance baseline; identified a potential energy-saving opportunity of ~55,440 kWh/year (~₹4.43 lakh/year), to be validated through airflow and power measurement before implementation.
Operated reliably with a consistent average load factor of 75% and stable delivery pressure of 6.7 kg/cm².
Primary corrective actions — inlet filter maintenance, leak detection, pressure optimisation, VSD controller verification — are low-cost, high-return, and require no capital investment.
Boiler
Average flue gas temperature of 205.9°C exceeded the boiler's own best-demonstrated 189.5°C by 16.4°C — a sustained, recoverable opportunity warranting further investigation.
Indicative ~0.75% thermal efficiency loss (BEE rule); no financial savings figure is stated, as fuel data was not independently verified and no direct efficiency test was conducted.
Recommended actions — economiser/APH cleaning, excess-air review, fuel metering, periodic KPI tracking — are low-cost and high-return; impact should be quantified via verified before/after measurement.
Both audits establish a systematic energy-monitoring baseline and point to practical, low-investment corrective actions. Extending the scope to distribution-network leak quantification, demand-side audit, and verified fuel/efficiency testing is recommended as the next phase.
